name: Denomination effect
statement: People are less willing to spend a sum held as one large note than the same sum in small notes, so a $20 bill survives a shop that twenty $1 bills would not.
meaning: Money is fungible, and a hundred in one note buys exactly what a hundred in five twenties buys. The claim is that holders do not treat the two as the same. A single large note is harder to break, so it sits in the wallet while loose small notes leave it. Two accounts of why compete, and they were published three years apart by different groups. Mishra, Mishra and Nayakankuppam proposed in 2006 that the whole is processed more fluently than the parts, that fluency produces positive affect, and that the affect inflates the note's perceived value. Raghubir and Srivastava proposed in 2009 that the large note is a self-control device: it is less psychologically fungible, so people who want to stop themselves spending choose to hold one. The two accounts predict opposite feelings about the money, and that is where the evidence splits. A second claim rides along with the first and is usually dropped in retelling. Breaking the note removes the barrier, so people who do spend a large note spend more of it than people spending small ones.

origin.note: The name comes from this paper. The finding does not: Mishra, Mishra and Nayakankuppam had reported a 'bias for the whole' in the same journal in 2006, across four experiments on spending intentions. Raghubir and Srivastava's contribution was to test actual purchases rather than intentions, and to argue for a different mechanism.

evidence: Raghubir and Srivastava report three studies. Study 1 has three parts. In 1a, 89 undergraduates at two American universities were given $1, either as four quarters or as a note, and offered candy. About 63% (27/43) bought in the quarters condition against 26% (12/46) with the note, chi-square(1) = 12.16, p < .001. Mean spending was $0.56 against $0.30. In 1b, 75 drivers at a filling station in Omaha were given $5 as five $1 notes, five $1 coins, or one $5 note. Non-fuel purchase rates were 24%, 12% and 16%. The denomination coefficient was marginal, b = -0.70, Wald = 3.20, p < .07, and the authors state that combining the two five-dollar-in-ones conditions leaves no reliable difference against the $5 note. In 1c, 150 women aged 25 to 45 in Xiangtan, China, were handed RMB 100 as one note or as five, and offered soap, shampoo, bedding, and pots and pans. Non-spending doubled from 9.3% (7/75) to 20% (15/75) under the single note, Fisher's exact test p < .05. Tests on the likelihood of spending were one-tailed. Study 2 asked 79 students to imagine a $100 focus-group payment; 73.81% chose five $20 notes when the scenario gave them no savings goal to protect, against 21.62% when it did. Study 3 gave 119 students the same choice and split them on the tightwad-spendthrift scale. Tightwads' choice of the single note rose from 20% (5/25) to 57.6% (19/33) with the need for self-control; spendthrifts sat at 51.4% and 50%.

replication.headline: Two independent tests exist. An Indonesian experiment with 240 students and 120 shoppers found no denomination effect on spending. An American field study of 154 people found one, but its p = .056 belongs to a three-condition test of payment form, not to denomination alone.
replication.detail: Bambang Juanda ran the effect against a proposed IDR 200,000 note, using two clipped IDR 100,000 notes as the large denomination and a mixed handful as the small one. The laboratory study recruited 240 students, but ran them as 80 groups of three, and the covariance model is fitted on those 80 observations rather than on the students. Its denomination main effect on spending was F(1, 63) = 0.216, p = .643. A quasi-experimental field study of 120 shoppers in the city and the regency of Bogor gave F(1, 99) = 0.379, p = .540. Price of goods, self-control and planning all moved spending in those models; denomination did not. Juanda's conclusion runs against the original in direction as well as size, reporting that field spending was higher with the large denomination. Every table and figure in the article is credited to Juanda (2015), an unpublished mimeo report to Bank Indonesia, so the 2018 article writes up an earlier commissioned study rather than fresh data. The nearest supportive independent test is Helen Colby's 2013 Rutgers dissertation, written under Gretchen Chapman and not published as an article. Its Study 5 paid 154 people at a New Jersey street fair $2, as a $2 note, as eight quarters in a sealed clear envelope, or as eight quarters loose in an open cup, and watched whether they played a nearby 25-cent ball game. Spending was $0.07, $0.11 and $0.27, F(2, 151) = 2.95, p = .056, with 5%, 16% and 20% of each group spending anything. That test compares three payment forms at once. The contrast that matters for the denomination account, note against loose coins, was t(109) = 2.34, p = .021. Colby reads the pattern as partitioning rather than fungibility or fluency, because the sealed envelope of coins behaved like the note.

study.cite: Juanda, B. (2018). The denomination effect on spending through experimental approach. Buletin Ekonomi Moneter dan Perbankan, 20(4), 461-496.

limits: The original evidence is thinner than its reputation. Every cell in study 1a holds about 45 people, and the money at stake is one dollar. Study 1b, the only part conducted on ordinary adults going about their day, produces the weakest result in the paper: marginal at p < .07, and absent once the coin and note versions of five dollars are pooled. Its follow-up analysis of how much spenders spent rests on the six, three and four people who bought in the three conditions, and is reported as F(6, 4) = 1.61, which the authors flag as unstable. The Halloween check involved 24 children, eleven of them in the note condition. Tests of spending likelihood were run one-tailed throughout. The largest sample, the 150 women in China, is the one where the aggregate result goes the other way: total spending was RMB 51.47 under small notes and RMB 54.13 under the single note, because the people who broke the big note spent more of it. Whether the effect survives outside cash is open. Reutskaja, Iyamabo, Raghubir and Gallo report that people prefer to pay with a denomination matching the price, and that this pushes them towards cash over card when a held note matches the price exactly. Li and Pandelaere report in their abstract that the effect reverses for expensive items, where buyers prefer to hand over the large note, and that the same matching carries over to gift cards. Zenkic, Lei, Millet and Rotman report a reversal again in tipping, where small denominations are tipped less often because handing them over is embarrassing. No source read here tests a card balance or a digital wallet.
misreadings: The phrase 'three field studies' comes from the paper's own abstract and does not match its own table. That table labels study 1a a laboratory study and 1c a simulated field study, run by a market research agency in a room. One of the three, study 1b, was a field study, and it is the weakest of them. The second misreading is that the two founding papers agree. They agree on the direction of spending and disagree on everything else. Raghubir and Srivastava tested Mishra and colleagues' affect mechanism twice and failed to find it both times, reporting all p's greater than .30 on the subjective perception scale in study 3. In China, satisfaction after buying was higher for the women given small notes, 3.60 against 3.23, which is the opposite of what a positive-affect account predicts. The third is that a large note reduces what you spend. It reduces whether you spend. Once the note is broken, the paper's own figures show spending going up: $1.17 against $0.82 in study 1a, RMB 67.67 against RMB 56.76 in study 1c. The advice to carry a hundred rather than five twenties rests on winning the first decision and losing the second.

Read in full on 2026-09-21, as an open copy of the typeset article carrying the journal's own pagination, at rofianto.wordpress.com; academic.oup.com and journals.uchicago.edu both answered with a Cloudflare challenge rather than a paywall that day. Every figure quoted on this page was checked against it.

Mishra, H., Mishra, A., & Nayakankuppam, D. (2006). Money: A bias for the whole. Journal of Consumer Research, 32(4), 541-549. The full text was not obtained on 2026-09-21. academic.oup.com and journals.uchicago.edu each answered with a Cloudflare interstitial, not a paywall notice; Crossref holds no abstract; Academia.edu and ResearchGate want a login. The four-experiment design and the fluency mechanism are taken from the publisher's abstract as deposited at RePEc, and from Raghubir and Srivastava's description of it.

Juanda, B. (2018). The denomination effect on spending through experimental approach. Buletin Ekonomi Moneter dan Perbankan, 20(4), 461-496. Read in full on 2026-09-21 as the journal's own PDF at bmeb-bi.org; the bulletin.bmeb-bi.org copy that indexes point to sits behind a Cloudflare challenge. Crossref gives pages 461-496; the article's own page headers run 493 to 528. Much of the PDF carries no character map, so the sampling and results pages were read as images.

Colby, H. (2013). A partitioning explanation of the denomination effect. PhD dissertation, Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey. Read in full from the Rutgers repository on 2026-09-21. No journal article of this work was found that day in Crossref or by plain search; an earlier three-study version was given as a 2011 conference paper, 'Don't break the $100 bill', which the Bayes Business School host served only through the Wayback Machine and which does not contain the street-fair study.

The reverse effect at high prices and the extension to gift cards are quoted from the abstract in Macquarie University's repository record, read that day.
